splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls the amount withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be finalized by the end of the prior plan year, providing employers greater predictability but potentially requiring use of older assumptions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and that judicial creation of such a doctrine exceeds courts' authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive collateral attack, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring relitigation of any previously presented claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to successive § 2255 motions, meaning federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome determines whether election rule disputes can be resolved before an election or must wait until after, with potentially chaotic consequences for election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office suffers a cognizable competitive injury from state election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes, giving the candidate Article III standing to challenge those rules before an election.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized grievance about election procedures is insufficient to confer Article III standing absent a concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision that allows courts to impose sentences below statutory minimums. This split results in defendants with identical criminal histories receiving different sentences depending on the circuit where they are sentenced.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations (including Sentencing Commission commentary) in the criminal context. This split has significant implications for how sentencing enhancements are applied and how ambiguous criminal statutes are construed post-Loper Bright.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as one of the oldest canons of interpretation, takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when a criminal sentencing provision is ambiguous.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions when supported by agency expertise.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and enforceable interpretation of the career-offender guideline.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses not mentioned in the guideline text. This split affects career-offender designations and substantially increases sentences for affected defendants.

positions.label: Commentary is valid — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor, and that conspiracy qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary is invalid — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond its text, so conspiracy does not qualify as a 'controlled substance offense.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), may be considered as a factor supporting 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive sentencing law changes as contributing to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits allow it, while others categorically bar it. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, may support a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes categorically barred
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's assets belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value during a Chapter 13 case becomes part of the bankruptcy estate when the case is converted to Chapter 7. This matters significantly to debtors who may lose substantial equity gains in their homes upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, and § 348(f)(1)(A) does not exclude such appreciation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, as the Bankruptcy Code's structure, object, and legislative history support protecting good-faith converting debtors from losing equity gains.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge conditions of confinement through habeas corpus or whether they may bring such claims as civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens), and whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or fact of confinement.
splits.description: Circuits have been split for decades on the scope of habeas corpus vs. civil rights remedies for prisoners challenging BOP decisions, including First Step Act time-credit determinations. The split affects whether prisoners must exhaust habeas requirements or can pursue civil claims for statutory violations related to their confinement.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement (including BOP decisions on early release and time credits), habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims (under Bivens or § 1983 for state prisoners) to challenge certain conditions or terms of confinement even when the claims touch on duration of custody.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to a Hyde Amendment order denying attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the 30-day criminal deadline or the 60-day civil deadline applies when appealing an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees. Most circuits treat it as a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but there is a minority view treating it as criminal.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines even if the substance involved is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender and other sentencing guideline provisions require that a prior state drug conviction involve a substance that is also controlled under federal law. This split affects base offense levels and career-offender designations for defendants with prior state convictions for substances not on the federal schedule.

positions.label: State-only controlled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that USSG § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include any offense under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Must be federally scheduled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for the violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentencing must be limited to the purposes specified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether revocation of supervised release may be used as a punitive measure. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split on the proper purpose of revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of trust and the statutory purposes of deterrence and protection of the public, not on punishing the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any ... broker,' extends to state-law negligence claims against freight brokers arising from motor carrier accidents. This affects the liability exposure of the freight brokerage industry.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's 'services' within the meaning of the statute.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted because they do not relate to the broker's prices, routes, or services in the relevant sense.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination in the operation of hospitality or business establishments, including the scope of liability and available remedies under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination claims in business establishments was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in the hospitality and service industries.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied certain standards governing discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found warranted review, suggesting a potentially erroneous or circuit-splitting approach.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards to discrimination claims in business establishments, creating a split that prompted SCOTUS to grant certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under § 2255 — such as claims of legal error in the original conviction or sentence — may also be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. This affects thousands of prisoners seeking sentence reductions.

positions.label: Such factors may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in the original conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Such factors may not be considered
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the legality of the original conviction or sentence must be raised through habeas proceedings and cannot serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
